extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; policymakers and historians of economic thought
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts principles and evaluative claims from an 18th-century treatise on political economy (Wealth of Nations), covering what constitutes productive labour, how national revenue and real wealth increase, the role of markets/trade, proper duties of the sovereign, and practical accounting for fisheries bounties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Productive vs unproductive labour
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificers, manufacturers, and merchants are classed among the productive labourers; menial servants among the barren or unproductive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when an artificer's consumption equals the value he produces over a given period, his labour adds to the annual produce because he converts consumed subsistence into work that can purchase subsistence for others; thus the market value existing at any moment is increased by such production. The text gives a six-month artificer example to show how production and consumption together raise the annual produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Savings from revenue increase real wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: If the revenue (fund destined for consumption) of a class equals the value of what they produce, what is naturally saved out of this revenue must necessarily increase the real wealth of the society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes that expressing revenue equality precisely (rather than consumption=production) clarifies that savings out of revenue augment the annual produce; criticisms of opponents' phrasing show this effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two ways to augment annual produce
rubrics_metrics.description: The annual produce of land and labour can be augmented only by (1) improvement in the productive powers of the useful labour actually maintained, or (2) an increase in the quantity of that labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improvement depends on the workman's ability and on his machinery. Because manufacturing labour can be more subdivided, it is more capable of such improvements (see book i chap. 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of useful labour depends on capital (savings)
rubrics_metrics.description: The increase in the quantity of useful labour actually employed depends on the increase of the capital which employs it; the increase of that capital must equal savings from revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If merchants, artificers, and manufacturers are more inclined to parsimony and saving than proprietors and cultivators, they will more likely augment useful labour and thereby increase real revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade/manufactures raise a country's subsistence and revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: A trading and manufacturing country can import, by means of trade and manufactures, a greater quantity of subsistence than its own lands could afford in their current cultivation; hence, other things equal, its revenue will be greater than that of one without trade or manufactures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A small quantity of manufactured produce purchases a great quantity of rude produce; thus towns (or trading nations) draw rude produce from countries to supply subsistence and materials of work. Examples include Holland importing cattle and corn and exporting manufactured goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of the market regulates division of labour and manufacturing perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of manufacturing industry depends on the division of labour, and the degree to which division of labour can be introduced is regulated by the extent of the market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large home or foreign markets allow greater subdivision of labour; China's vast home market can support considerable subdivisions and manufactures, but more extensive foreign trade and navigation would further increase Chinese manufactures and their productive powers by exposing them to foreign machines and improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systems of preference or restraint misallocate capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Any system that, by extraordinary encouragements or restraints, tries to draw more or less capital to a particular species of industry than would naturally go to it is subversive of its own ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such systems retard progress toward real wealth by forcing capital into less advantageous uses or out of advantageous ones; agricultural-preferring systems that restrain manufactures end up discouraging agriculture itself, while mercantile systems at least encourage the targeted industry in the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural liberty and the limited duties of the sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the system of natural liberty the sovereign has only three duties: (1) protect the society from violence and invasion of other independent societies; (2) protect every member from injustice or oppression by others (establish administration of justice); and (3) erect and maintain public works and public institutions that cannot be profitably provided by individuals or small groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These duties are of great importance but are plain and intelligible; attempts by the sovereign to superintend private industry expose him to delusions and are unsuitable because no human wisdom could direct private industry better than individuals pursuing their own interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public expense requires revenue and analysis of taxation/debt
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper performance of the sovereign's duties supposes a certain expense which requires revenue; one must explain (1) necessary expenses of the sovereign and which should be defrayed by the whole society or particular parts, (2) different methods for the whole society to contribute and their advantages/inconveniences, and (3) reasons governments mortgage part of revenue or contract debts and the effects of those debts on real wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This passage functions as an organizational criterion for public finance analysis, signaling that taxation incidence, methods of raising revenue, and effects of public debt are central topics to be evaluated in the following book/chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slavery and caste systems undermine manufacturing efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: In societies where many trades are carried on by slaves, such manufactures are generally executed with more labour and higher expense than when carried on by freemen who introduce machinery and improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slaves are seldom inventive; freemen introduce machinery and improved arrangements of work. Historical examples: Turkish mines wrought by slaves were costlier than Hungarian ones; ancient manufactures (silk, linen) often very dear, partly due to awkward machinery and the absence of inventive freemen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting method for tonnage bounty to the white-herring fishery (appendix example)
rubrics_metrics.description: A detailed accounting method for computing the government bounty on barrels of herrings landed by Scottish busses, including counting number of busses, empty barrels carried out, barrels of herrings caught, and computing bounty per barrel after adjustments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The appendix provides numerical tables (years, number of busses, empty barrels, barrels caught, bounty paid), conversions (sea-sticks to fully packed barrels by counting a sea-stick barrel as two-thirds of a fully packed barrel), deductions for partially packed barrels (one third deducted), addition of export premiums, and adjustments adding duties of salt used in curing (foreign or British salt) to compute effective bounty per barrel under different cases (exported vs entered for home consumption). The passage shows how to translate raw catches and raw bounties into per-barrel monetary figures with multiple step adjustments.
